title: Deuteronomy
subtitle: These are the words
lead: Deuteronomy is called in Hebrew Devarim, "Words," from its first line: "These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel" (1:1). Its English name comes from the Greek Deuteronomion, "second law," after the Septuagint's rendering of the king's "copy of this law" (17:18). The rabbis also called it Mishneh Torah, "the repetition of the law." The whole book is set on a single day or a few weeks at the end of the fortieth year, on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho. Moses, who will not enter the land, speaks to the children of the generation that came out of Egypt.

The book is mostly speeches. In the first (1:1–4:43) Moses retells the journey from Horeb and draws its lesson: the LORD alone is God, heard but not seen. The second and longest (4:44–28:68) repeats the Ten Words, gives the Shema, "Listen, Israel" (6:4), and sets out the laws for life in the land, from one place of worship to the care of slaves, widows and foreigners, ending with blessings and curses. The third (29–30) renews the covenant and sets life and death before the people. The last chapters hand over leadership to Joshua, give Moses' Song and his blessing of the tribes, and tell of his death on Mount Nebo.

Deuteronomy is one of the most quoted books in the Bible. Its language of love, choice, memory and the heart shaped the prophets and the history books from Joshua to Kings. Jews recite its words every morning and evening and fix them to their doors. Jesus answered the devil from it three times and called its command to love God the first of all. Critical scholars see in it the scroll that sparked King Josiah's reform, and nearly everyone reads it against the treaties of the ancient Near East.
facts: Not named except as the speaker. Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses (with the account of his death added by Joshua or another). Most critical scholars: Judean scribes of the 7th century BC and the exile.
Set in the fortieth year after the exodus. Critical: a core under King Josiah (about 622 BC), expanded in the exile.
The plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, near Beth-peor and Mount Nebo
Speeches and sermons, laws, a covenant ceremony, a song and a blessing, and a short narrative frame

audience.to: The book speaks to two audiences at once. Inside the story, Moses speaks to all Israel on the plains of Moab at the end of the fortieth year. They are the children of the generation that left Egypt and died in the wilderness. They are about to cross the Jordan without him. Outside the story, the first readers depend on the view of authorship. On the traditional view, they are Israel in the land after Moses' death. On the critical view, they are the people of Judah under King Josiah about 622 BC, and then the exiles in Babylon after 586 BC.
audience.why: To set the terms of life in the land before Israel enters it. There is one God, to be loved with the whole heart, and one place to worship him. The laws bind every household, the judges, the priests and Levites, the prophets and even the king. They protect the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. Moses keeps saying "today." So every later generation hears the covenant as made with them (5:3; 29:14–15). Knowing the audience changes the reading. It is a sermon to people about to gain land, wealth and kings, warning them not to forget the God who gave them. For readers who had lost the land, it explains why. It also promises a way back if they return with all their heart (4:25–31; 30:1–10).
views: Traditional: Moses to the generation entering the land

The speeches are Moses' own, written down by him and given to the priests and Levites (31:9, 24–26), with the account of his death added later. The first readers are Israel in the land in the time of Joshua and the judges. They were to hear the law read aloud every seventh year at the Feast of Booths (31:10–13). Scholars such as Kline, Craigie and Kitchen point to the treaty form of the late second millennium BC.

Since de Wette (1805), most critical scholars link the core of the book with the "scroll of the law" found in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kings 22:8). That core is chapters 12–26, with 5–11 and 28. Its first readers were Judah a century after the northern kingdom fell, under Assyrian power. Josiah's reform does what the book asks: one place of worship, the end of the high places, a national Passover. Its language of loyalty and its curses echo the oaths the Assyrian king Esarhaddon imposed in 672 BC. So the book tells Judah that it owes this loyalty to the LORD alone. Speaking in Moses' voice gave the reform the authority of the founder. Some scholars place the first core a little earlier, under Hezekiah, who also closed the high places (2 Kings 18:4). Others, such as Juha Pakkala, argue that the law code has no real king in view and was written after the monarchy ended.

Many scholars think the frame (chapters 1–4 and 29–30) was added in the exile after 586 BC, as the opening of the history from Joshua to Kings. Its readers were once again outside the land, like Israel on the plains of Moab. To them the book explains the disaster as the covenant's curses and holds out a return if they take the words to heart.

Others (von Rad, Weinfeld, and many since) think the book's traditions began in the northern kingdom, among Levites or prophets like Hosea. They were carried to Judah after 722 BC. On this view the ceremony at Mounts Ebal and Gerizim near Shechem (11:29; 27) keeps an old northern covenant rite.

lenses.name: Moses' farewell
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Moses gave these speeches on the plains of Moab just before his death, and the book (apart from the account of his death) comes from him.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars link the core of Deuteronomy (chapters 12–26) to the scroll found in the temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22), shaped in the 7th century BC and expanded during the exile, as the base of a 'Deuteronomistic History' running through Kings.

lenses.name: Covenant treaty
lenses.desc: Many scholars of every school read the book's shape (history, laws, blessings and curses, witnesses) against ancient Near Eastern treaties: Hittite treaties of the 2nd millennium BC (Kitchen, Kline) or Assyrian loyalty oaths of Esarhaddon from 672 BC (Weinfeld, Levinson).

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis call it Devarim, 'Words', and Mishneh Torah, 'the repetition of the Law'. The Shema (6:4–9) is said twice daily, and the Sifre, the Talmud, Rashi and Ramban read its laws as the heart of Jewish practice.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Jesus answers each of his three temptations from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4) and names 6:5 the greatest commandment. The New Testament reads the 'prophet like me' (18:15) as Jesus, and Paul reads the law's curse and the word 'near you' (30:14) through Christ (Galatians 3; Romans 10).

authorship: The book presents itself as Moses' words, and says that Moses put this law in writing and gave it to the priests (31:9) and to the Levites to keep beside the ark (31:24–26). Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a) and the church fathers took Moses as author of the whole Torah, with Joshua writing the last eight verses on his death. Conservative scholars such as Peter Craigie, Daniel Block and Kenneth Kitchen point to the book's form, which they compare to Hittite treaties of about 1400–1200 BC, and to its desert setting and its point of view from east of the Jordan.

In 1805 W. M. L. de Wette argued that Deuteronomy is the "book of the law" found in the temple under King Josiah in 622 BC (2 Kings 22–23). Josiah's reform matches Deuteronomy's demands closely: one place of worship, the destruction of high places, a national Passover, the ban on standing stones and Asherah poles. Most critical scholars still hold that the core of the book, chapters 12–26, was written or revised in Judah in the late 8th or 7th century BC, perhaps by Levites, prophets or court scribes, drawing on older northern traditions.

Martin Noth (1943) proposed that Deuteronomy 1–3 (or 1–4) was written as the opening of one long history running through Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, composed in the exile to explain the fall of Israel and Judah. Frank Moore Cross and others see two editions, one under Josiah and one in the exile. Many now see Deuteronomy itself as growing in layers, with the frame of chapters 1–11 and 27–34 added around the laws.

Since George Mendenhall (1955) scholars have compared Deuteronomy with ancient treaties. Meredith Kline and Kenneth Kitchen argue that its shape (preamble, history, stipulations, deposit, witnesses, blessings and curses) best fits Hittite treaties of the late 2nd millennium BC, supporting an early date. Moshe Weinfeld and Bernard Levinson point to close parallels with the loyalty oaths of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (672 BC), including curses in the same order, and date the book to the 7th century. Some see both: an old covenant form taken up and recast in Assyrian times.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. It is built line by line from the Hebrew words in their own order rather than adapted from another English version. YHWH is "the LORD," and Adonai YHWH is "Lord GOD." Deuteronomy's own vocabulary of law is kept steady: chuqqim are "rules," mishpatim "rulings," mitsvah "command," 'edot "decrees," and torah "law," with the notes pointing out that it also means "instruction." The Ten Commandments are "the Ten Words," as the Hebrew says. Cherem is "under the ban"; ger is "foreigner"; segullah is "own private treasure"; to'evah is "abhorrent"; nachalah is "inheritance"; yarash is "take possession of" a land or "drive out" a people; dabaq is to "hold on to" God. Nefesh is "being" (not "soul"), and hesed is "loyal love." In the Ten Words, chamad is "crave" and hit'avveh "long for." These renderings are shared with the rest of the site.

Moses' speeches are printed inside quotation marks, and the narrator's asides about ancient peoples and places (for example 2:10–12, 2:20–23, 3:9, 3:11, 3:13–14, 10:6–9) are set in parentheses. The Song of Moses (chapter 32) and the Blessing of Moses (chapter 33) are set as verse.

Where the Masoretic Text differs from the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint or the Dead Sea Scrolls in a way that matters, the variant is shown beside the verse. Examples are the Samaritan command about Mount Gerizim added to the Ten Words, the order of the commands about murder and adultery in the Greek, and the readings of the Song of Moses in chapter 32.

KJV, ASV, WEB, YLT

Public-domain English versions. The KJV (1611, standard text of 1769) prints words the translators added in italics. Young's Literal Translation (1898) keeps Hebrew word order and tenses.

BSB

The Berean Standard Bible, a modern translation released into the public domain.

Hebrew

The Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), as edited by the Westminster Leningrad Codex project and corrected in STEPBible's TAHOT (Tyndale House, Cambridge), with each word's meaning and grammar. English Bibles number a few verses differently from the Hebrew (12:32 is Hebrew 13:1, 22:30 is 23:1, 29:1 is 28:69); this site follows the English numbering.

Deuteronomy is preaching. Moses does not simply list laws; he urges, warns, explains and pleads, and the book's favorite words show it: "today," "remember," "do not forget," "love," "with all your heart." Three keys help.

First, listen for "today." The generation in front of Moses was not at Horeb, but he tells them, "The LORD did not make this covenant with our ancestors. He made it with us, we who are here today, all of us alive" (5:3). Every new generation is meant to hear the book the same way.

Second, follow the structure. The book's headings mark its parts: "These are the words" (1:1), "This is the law" (4:44), the words of the covenant in Moab (29:1), "This is the blessing" (33:1). The laws of chapters 12–26 roughly follow the order of the Ten Words, as Jewish commentators and modern scholars such as Stephen Kaufman have noticed.

Third, notice the choice. Again and again Moses sets two roads before the people: blessing and curse (11:26), life and death. The book closes with Moses dying outside the land, so that the choice passes to the people and to Joshua.

In the 1950s scholars noticed that Deuteronomy is shaped like a treaty between a great king and a lesser king. Hittite treaties of about 1400–1200 BC have a preamble naming the king, a history of what he has done for his vassal, the terms of loyalty, instructions to deposit the document and read it regularly, a list of divine witnesses, and blessings and curses. Deuteronomy has all of these: the speaker and setting (1:1–5), the history (1:6–4:49), the main command and the laws (5–26), the tablets in the ark and the public reading of the law (10:1–5; 31:9–13), heaven and earth as witnesses (4:26; 30:19), and blessings and curses (27–28).

Assyrian loyalty oaths, above all those Esarhaddon imposed in 672 BC, are even closer in places: they command the vassals to "love" the crown prince, to teach their sons, to report anyone who incites rebellion, even a prophet or a relative (compare chapter 13), and they list curses very like those of chapter 28. Scholars who date Deuteronomy early stress the Hittite form; those who date it late stress the Assyrian wording. Either way, the comparison shows what the book claims: Israel's covenant is a treaty with God as its only king.

In the synagogue Deuteronomy is read in eleven weekly portions from midsummer to the autumn feasts, ending on Simchat Torah, when the last verses are read and Genesis 1 is begun at once. Its first portion falls just before the Ninth of Av. The book is the source of much daily Jewish practice: the Shema (6:4–9; 11:13–21), said morning and evening; tefillin and the mezuzah (6:8–9); grace after meals (8:10); and many laws of the festivals, tithes, charity and marriage. The Sifre on Deuteronomy, a legal midrash, and the later Deuteronomy Rabbah are its main rabbinic commentaries, followed by Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban. Maimonides named his great law code Mishneh Torah after the book. The rabbis read its stern warnings and its promises of return together, and the words "It is not in heaven" (see 30:12) became, in a famous story of the Talmud, a basic principle of how the law is interpreted (Bavli Bava Metzia 59b).

Deuteronomy is quoted or alluded to in the New Testament more than almost any other book of the Old Testament. Jesus answers each of the devil's temptations from Deuteronomy 6–8 (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13) and names the Shema as the first commandment (Mark 12:28–34). Peter and Stephen identify the "prophet like me" of 18:15 with Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37). Paul reads the curse on one hanged on a tree (21:23) as the curse Christ bore (Galatians 3:13), and the word "near you" (30:14) as the message of faith (Romans 10:6–8). Hebrews draws on the warnings of the wilderness and the fire at Horeb (Hebrews 3–4; 12:18–29). Church fathers read the laws both literally and as signs of spiritual truths, and the Reformers used the book to teach the Ten Commandments and the place of the law in Christian life.

Deuteronomy was one of the most copied books at Qumran: about thirty manuscripts of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, more than of any book except the Psalms. Some, such as 4QDeut-n and the scrolls used in tefillin, contain only selected passages, such as the Ten Words and the Shema, and mix in wording from Exodus. The Nash Papyrus, a single sheet from Egypt of about 150–100 BC, has the Ten Words and the Shema together. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim after the Ten Words, and reads "Gerizim" for "Ebal" in 27:4. In the Song of Moses (chapter 32) the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint preserve readings, such as "the sons of God" in 32:8, that many scholars think older than the Masoretic Text. The variant notes beside the text show these places.

spec.title: Deuteronomy as a book of 'today'
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Deuteronomy is built to collapse time. Moses speaks to the children as if they were the parents ("you" stood at Horeb, "you" refused at Kadesh), and he speaks of a covenant made "today" with "we who are here today, all of us alive" (5:3), and later with those not yet born as well (29:14–15). The Hebrew word hayyom, "today," appears dozens of times in the book. The effect is that every reading of the book becomes the moment of decision on the plains of Moab. That would explain why the law was to be read aloud every seven years (see 31:10–13), why the Shema is said every day, and why the book ends with Moses' death outside the land: the speaker is gone, and the hearers are left with the choice. Gerhard von Rad and others have written on "today" in Deuteronomy; the suggestion that the whole design, including Moses' death, serves this collapse of time is my own.

An old man with a long white beard and a staff stands on a low rise of ground, speaking with one hand raised. Before him a vast crowd of men, women and children sits and stands among tents on a broad plain. Behind them a river winds through a green strip, and beyond it, far off, a walled town among palm trees and hills rising in the haze.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment, never a hard rectangular frame.

Moshe Weinfeld, Deuteronomy 1–11 (Anchor Bible, 1991) and Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School (1972)
The classic critical studies, strong on the treaty parallels and the book's links with wisdom and the scribes.
Peter C. Craigie, The Book of Deuteronomy (NICOT, 1976)
A clear evangelical commentary that reads the book as a covenant document of Moses' time.
A full critical commentary on the book's growth and themes.
Reads the book as Moses' sermons, with attention to its message for Christians today.

How Deuteronomy rewrote older laws while claiming to repeat them.

A careful study of what the Shema and chapter 4 claim about God.
